prompt: What does the Baker/baker paradox describe?
options: The same word is easier to recall as a job than as a surname
Bakers are unusually good at remembering names
Surnames are easier to recall than jobs when they are the same word
People mix up surnames that sound alike
correctAnswer: The same word is easier to recall as a job than as a surname
explanation: It is much harder to recall that a person's surname is Baker than that a person is a baker, because the job comes with meaning and the name does not.

prompt: Most people rate their own memory for names as better than average, just as they do for most other abilities.
explanation: False. In Hargis, Whatley and Castel's 2020 study, people rated themselves better than average on most items, but rated their memory for names as about the same as everyone else's. Struggling with names is the norm, not a personal flaw.

prompt: Baseline drill: the young man with a ginger beard and freckles was Mr _____.
explanation: He was Mr Mason, a nurse. If you remembered "nurse" but not "Mason", that is the Baker/baker paradox in action.

prompt: Baseline drill: match each person to their job.

pairs.left: A tall man with a shaved head and a gold earring
A woman with grey plaits and round glasses
An old man with bushy white eyebrows
A woman with long black hair and dimples

explanation: Pilot, baker, judge and teacher: Mr Potter, Mrs Hughes, Mr Fisher and Mrs Shepherd. Most people find the jobs easier to recall than the names.

prompt: You remember that a colleague works in accounts and that you met at the gym, but not her name. What does the face-to-name route in this lesson say is happening?
options: You have reached who she is, but her name sits in a separate store further along
Her face was never stored in memory
Your memory for faces has failed
The name is stored with the face, so you should stare harder
correctAnswer: You have reached who she is, but her name sits in a separate store further along
explanation: You have reached who she is, but the name sits in a separate store at the end of the chain. Craigie and Hanley found that recalling a name from a face depended on recalling the occupation first.

prompt: In Brenner's 1973 experiment, readers recalled worst the words read by others shortly before their own turn.
explanation: True. Recall dropped for words read shortly before the reader's own turn, starting three words before it, while listeners showed no dip. Brenner called it the next-in-line effect.

prompt: Which step in this account of how you get from a face to a name is wrong?
steps: You see a face and it feels familiar
You reach who the person is: her job, where you met
From there you reach her name, held in a separate store
Because the face links straight to the name, you can skip the step about who she is
So you can often recall a job with no name attached
explanation: There is no direct link from a face to a name. The route runs through who the person is, which is why you can often recall a job without the name.

prompt: A meeting opens with everyone introducing themselves round the table, and you are sixth. Which names are you most likely to lose, and why?
options: The two or three just before yours, because you are preparing what to say
The first ones, because they were said longest ago
The ones after yours, because you are relieved and stop listening
None of them, as long as you are sitting at the table
correctAnswer: The two or three just before yours, because you are preparing what to say
explanation: The next-in-line effect: as your turn approaches, you are busy preparing your own words, so the names just before yours are poorly taken in. Decide what you will say before the round starts.

prompt: Which three parts did McCarty find were all essential to the face-name method?
options: A sound-alike for the name, a prominent facial feature, and an image joining them
Repeating the name, spelling it and writing it down
A rhyme, a song and a story
The person's job, home town and hobby
correctAnswer: A sound-alike for the name, a prominent facial feature, and an image joining them
explanation: With all three parts, recall was 55 per cent; with only some of them it was 12 to 23 per cent, no better than simply repeating and spelling the names.

prompt: Once you have learned the face-name method, it reliably improves name recall during real conversations.
explanation: False. Patton found it did not improve recall when attempted during real conversations, and at Morris and colleagues' 2005 party the imagery group recalled 12 per cent, no better than the 16 per cent of guests with no method.

prompt: Name-face drill: the man with a deep cleft in his chin was Mr _____.
explanation: Mr Kowalski. A cow on skis sliding into the cleft is one way to hook it; your own image is better.

prompt: Name-face drill: match each feature to the name.
explanation: Lockwood had the curly eyebrows, Sandford the ears that stick out, Penrose the rosy cheeks and Hammond the square jaw.

prompt: You meet a Mr Fairweather wearing a bright yellow hat, and he has wide-set eyes. Where should you pin your image?
options: On his wide-set eyes
On the yellow hat, since it stands out most
On his name badge
On the room where you met him
explanation: On the face. Carney and Levin found extra details beat facial features only when the test used the same picture; once the detail was gone, facial features won. Hats come off; eyes stay.

prompt: In Yesavage, Rose and Bower's study, adding a judgement of how pleasant each image was improved recall after 48 hours.
explanation: True. With the judgement, recall after 48 hours was 32 per cent, against 15 per cent for the standard method.

prompt: You see Mr Smolensky again. Put the steps of recalling his name in order.
steps: Look at his face and spot the broad nose
The nose brings back the skier taking pictures on it
The image gives you the sound-alike: small lens ski
The sound-alike gives you the name: Smolensky
explanation: Recall runs the method backwards: feature, then image, then sound-alike, then name. McCarty found the weakest link is retrieving the image.

prompt: A friend tries the face-name method on Mr Bryant. Which step undermines it?
steps: Hears "Bryant" and asks how it is spelled
Turns Bryant into "bride ant"
Notices his round cheeks
Pictures a bride ant, and separately pictures the cheeks, side by side
Later looks at the cheeks to bring the image back
explanation: The two images must interact. McCarty found that every part was essential, including the image that joins the sound-alike to the feature; two pictures side by side do not do that job.

prompt: Landauer and Bjork noted that at a party you cannot write names down. What did they suggest instead?
options: Test yourself on each name silently, again and again
Repeat each name aloud ten times straight away
Ask everyone to say their name again later
Write the names on your hand
correctAnswer: Test yourself on each name silently, again and again
explanation: Test yourself silently, again and again. An expanding schedule beat even gaps with the same average spacing in their experiments.

prompt: Hearing a name repeated as often as you would recall it works just as well as recalling it.
explanation: False. Name game players recalled 60 to 65 per cent after a half-hour seminar; people who heard the same names just as often recalled about 30 per cent.

prompt: Name game drill: put the first five people at the table in the order they introduced themselves.
steps: Priya, sailing
Tom, bees
Aled, rugby
Grace, jazz
Kenji, baking
explanation: Priya, Tom, Aled, Grace, Kenji. Running them backwards after each new arrival is what fixed the order.

prompt: Name game drill: the person who loves chess was _____.
explanation: Fatima, sixth at the table, between Kenji and Rory.

prompt: Why did Morris and Fritz reverse the name game, so that each player recalls the newest name first?
options: So the newest name is tested before it can be lost behind all the others
So the first person to speak gets the most practice
Because players found it more fun
To shorten the game for large groups
correctAnswer: So the newest name is tested before it can be lost behind all the others
explanation: In the original order, the most recently introduced name had to wait behind all the others and could be lost. The reversed game beat the original, 62 to 50 per cent.

prompt: Match each party move to the reason it works.

pairs.left: Saying the name back at once
pairs.right: Words you say aloud are remembered better

pairs.left: Asking where the name comes from
pairs.right: It gives a bare label some meaning

pairs.left: Testing after a minute, then later

explanation: Saying a name aloud helps it stick, a question adds meaning, spaced tests are retrieval practice, and running the names newest first protects the most fragile one.

prompt: At a conference dinner you will meet eight people in an hour. Which plan best fits the evidence?
options: Say each name back, test yourself soon and again later, and run the names backwards as people join
Build a detailed image for every face before replying to anything they say
Listen carefully once and trust your memory
Ask everyone to repeat their name several times
correctAnswer: Say each name back, test yourself soon and again later, and run the names backwards as people join
explanation: In real conversation, testing yourself is what works: say the name back, test early and again later, and run the names backwards as new people arrive. Building an image for every face is too slow mid-conversation.

prompt: Which statement about the name-learning research is wrong?
steps: Practising recall beat simply seeing the names again, 42 to 17 per cent
Thinking about what a name means added to the benefit of testing
Every study since 1978 has found expanding gaps better than even gaps
Spaced tests beat crammed tests
The reversed name game improved learning even in groups of about 25
explanation: The advantage of expanding gaps over even gaps is less clear than it first looked: several studies found no difference. What holds up is that spaced tests beat crammed ones.

prompt: In the keyword method, what is the keyword?
options: A word in your own language that sounds like part of the foreign word
The English translation of the foreign word
The same word in a third language
The most important word in a sentence
correctAnswer: A word in your own language that sounds like part of the foreign word
explanation: The keyword is a word in your own language that sounds like part of the foreign word, such as "dawn" in zdanie. It is the first, acoustic link.

prompt: Dunlosky and colleagues' 2013 review rated the keyword mnemonic one of the most useful study techniques.
explanation: False. They rated it low utility: hard to use in some contexts, and helpful for a limited range of material, with benefits they judged short-lived. Atkinson and Raugh's six-week result shows that last point is debated.

prompt: Keyword drill: the Spanish word maleta means _____.
explanation: Maleta means suitcase; the keyword was "mallet". Picture someone hammering a stuffed suitcase shut with a mallet.

prompt: Keyword drill: match each Spanish word to its meaning.
explanation: Gusano is worm (goose), hilo is thread (eel), trigo is wheat (tree) and jabón is soap (bone).

prompt: You want to learn the Russian persik, peach. Which keyword and image follow Atkinson's rules best?
options: "Pierre is sick": a Frenchman ill from eating too many peaches
"Peach", since it means the same
"Fruit", since a peach is a fruit
"Persian cat", asleep on a sofa
correctAnswer: "Pierre is sick": a Frenchman ill from eating too many peaches
explanation: "Pierre is sick" sounds like persik, and a Frenchman ill from eating peaches ties it to the meaning. "Peach" and "fruit" are links of meaning, not sound, and a sleeping cat has nothing to do with peaches.

prompt: In Atkinson and Raugh's Russian study, the keyword group's advantage had vanished by the surprise test six weeks later.
explanation: False. Six weeks later the keyword group still recalled 43 per cent of the words against 28 per cent for the control group.

prompt: Put the keyword method in order for the Russian zdanie, building.
steps: Hear the word: zdanie, said roughly "zdon-yeh"
Find a keyword that sounds like part of it: dawn
Picture dawn's pink light reflected in the windows of a tall building
Later, hear zdanie, think of dawn, and the image gives you building
explanation: First the acoustic link (zdanie sounds like dawn), then the imagery link (dawn lighting a building); recall runs along the same chain.

prompt: In one of Raugh and Atkinson's Spanish tests, the keyword "bale" for libélula, dragonfly, did worse than no keyword at all. What is the best lesson?
options: A poorly fitting keyword can hurt, so choose or change keywords with care
The keyword method does not work for Spanish
Keywords only work for short words
Control groups always do better with insects
correctAnswer: A poorly fitting keyword can hurt, so choose or change keywords with care
explanation: A keyword that does not fit can hurt: 20 per cent of the keyword group recalled libélula against 60 per cent of the controls. Choose keywords with care, and change one that keeps failing.

prompt: What did Quintilian advise for learning a long speech by heart?
options: Learn it piecemeal, in sections that are not too short
Read it straight through many times in one sitting
Learn it from a copy in someone else's handwriting
Learn it in complete silence
correctAnswer: Learn it piecemeal, in sections that are not too short
explanation: Learn it piecemeal, since nothing is so bad for memory as being overburdened, but not in sections so short that they break it up.

prompt: It has been shown that the phrase "in the first place" comes from the memory palace.
explanation: False. The story is often repeated but comes with no evidence, and Latin already used primo loco for "in the first place, first in order". Possible, but unproven.

prompt: Toast drill: put the first five beats in order.
steps: Thank everyone for coming
How you met: a broken-down bus
The camping trip in the rain
Her first terrible car
The move to Glasgow
explanation: Thanks, the broken-down bus, the camping trip, the terrible car, the move to Glasgow. Walking your route in order hands them back.

prompt: Toast drill: the sixth beat was the famous burnt _____.
explanation: The burnt lasagne, just before "What she means to her friends" and "Raise your glasses".

prompt: What curious fact about a single night did Quintilian report?
options: It greatly strengthens memory, so what would not come on the spot comes easily the next day
It wipes out most of what was learned that day
It makes no difference to memory either way
It helps only with poetry, not with prose
correctAnswer: It greatly strengthens memory, so what would not come on the spot comes easily the next day
explanation: He wrote that the interval of a single night greatly increases the strength of the memory, so things that could not be recalled on the spot come easily the next day. Hence: sleep on your speech.

prompt: Professional actors mostly learn their lines by rote repetition rather than by working out what the lines mean.
explanation: False. Actors recall text word for word using a meaning-based strategy, paying minute attention to exact wording and punctuation to work out the deep meaning.

prompt: A friend prepares a best-man speech. Which step goes against the advice in this lesson?
steps: Learns the opening and closing lines word for word
Cuts the middle into beats, each with an image on a route
Rehearses aloud, on his feet
Rereads the whole speech twenty times the night before instead of testing himself
Sleeps on it and runs through it once more the next day
explanation: Rereading wastes time on passages you already know; Quintilian advised testing yourself instead. The other steps follow the lesson.

prompt: Match each source to what this lesson took from it.

pairs.right: Repeats the "first place" story as fact
Latin primo loco: first in order

explanation: Quintilian noticed the overnight boost; the Noices showed actors learn through meaning; Sarma's essay repeats the "first place" story; Lewis and Short show Latin primo loco meant first in order.
